date_cases.name: a date that ran is not unanalysed
date_cases.why: It is a row in runs[]; carrying it here too would put one day on both lists.

date_cases.name: a quiet date that ran is not unanalysed either
date_cases.why: zero_alerts is a positive observation of absence (green_release.classify_date), not a missing one.

date_cases.name: a date refused by the anomaly gate
date_cases.why: 2026-01-02 in the live release: more than 30% of the valid area flagged at once.

date_cases.name: a date refused for low coverage, twice
date_cases.why: Two acquisitions, both below 20% valid: one reason, not two — the reason is the status, not the count.

date_cases.name: mixed reasons are sorted
date_cases.why: The index is reproducible byte for byte; the order cannot depend on the order of status_counts.

date_cases.name: a date with no usable acquisition and no status is refused
date_cases.why: classify_date cannot produce it. Showing it with an invented reason would be the site explaining what the ledger did not.

date_cases.name: a sealing status on an unanalysed date is refused
date_cases.why: A complete_* acquisition makes a date usable. If the release says no_valid_coverage anyway, the two disagree and neither is shown.

index_cases.name: no runs is a legitimate index
index_cases.why: The state before the first release. last_run is null and pcount_max falls back to the floor; refusing this state would make the site fail on a correct, empty green release.

index_cases.name: totals aggregate rows whose features were never supplied
index_cases.why: THE point of the design: every totals field is a function of the rows alone, so a consumer verifies the whole document without reading 429k features. If any total needed a feature, this case could not be built.

index_cases.name: the total area sums values already rounded
index_cases.why: Three rows at .05 sum to a different number depending on whether the rounding happened per row or once at the end. The per-row value is what a reader can add up by hand, so it is the one that is summed.

index_cases.name: pcount_max is the maximum of the rows, not of the last one
index_cases.why: The largest streak may belong to any date. Taking the last row's value would shrink the UI slider whenever the newest run happens to be quiet.

index_cases.name: unanalysed dates are carried, and touch no total and no last_run
index_cases.why: PHASE_6O §4. The live release had 61 of 103 dates with no usable acquisition, and the index dropped every one. They are carried now, beside runs[] and not in it: the latest date here is unanalysed, and last_run still names the latest date that RAN.

note: Neither the Python authority nor the site's composer is the reference: this file is. Add a case to the generator and regenerate; never hand-edit.

object_cases.name: the strong suffix is tested before the full suffix
object_cases.why: run-<date>.strong.geojson also ends in .geojson. Testing in the other order classifies the subset as the full run — silently — and the page's default view becomes every candidate alert.

object_cases.name: declaration order does not decide the answer
object_cases.why: The same two paths listed the other way round must classify identically, or the index depends on how the release happened to serialise its list.

object_cases.name: an unrelated object on the date is ignored
object_cases.why: A date may declare acquisition artifacts and other products. Only the two alert objects are the index's input.

object_cases.name: the assembler's prefix is not constrained
object_cases.why: The requirement is a suffix, deliberately the weakest one that works, so the run assembler stays free to choose its layout.

object_cases.name: no strong subset fails closed
object_cases.why: Falling back to the full object would serve 429k features as the default view while reporting the strong count.

object_cases.name: no full run fails closed
object_cases.why: The download link and the 'ver todos' view both address it.

object_cases.name: two full runs on one date fail closed
object_cases.why: There is no obvious winner, and picking one would make the index depend on list order.

object_cases.name: a date with no objects fails closed
object_cases.why: A date whose alert_state is 'alerts' must publish at least one object (GREEN_RELEASE_CONTRACT_V1 §3, product completeness), so an empty paths list here means the release and the index disagree.

rejection_cases.name: the persistence tiers no longer partition the count
rejection_cases.why: A tier gained a feature the count never had; the page would show more confirmed alerts than alerts.

rejection_cases.name: the confidence labels no longer partition the count
rejection_cases.why: Dropping a label bin loses features silently — the totals still look plausible because high is unchanged.

rejection_cases.name: strong exceeds the high-confidence features it is drawn from
rejection_cases.why: Strong membership requires the high label, so strong > high is arithmetically impossible and means the subset was computed against a different rule than the one reported.

rejection_cases.name: runs are not in chronological order
rejection_cases.why: The release's dates[] is required to be chronological. The site reads runs[len-1] as the latest run, so a reversed index shows the OLDEST date as the newest detection.

rejection_cases.name: last_run does not name the last row
rejection_cases.why: Two places in the page disagree about which run is current: the caption reads last_run and the map reads runs[len-1].

rejection_cases.name: a total does not aggregate its rows
rejection_cases.why: The all-runs headline number is the one figure a reader cannot check against anything else on the page.

rejection_cases.name: the total area was recomputed at a different precision
rejection_cases.why: Reproducibility, not tidiness: an index derived from the same immutable release must be byte-identical, and a stray decimal means two builds of one release disagree.

rejection_cases.name: the full object and the strong subset are the same object
rejection_cases.why: The default view would serve every candidate alert — 429k features instead of 125k, and a claim of high confidence the data does not carry.

rejection_cases.name: a UTC date appears twice
rejection_cases.why: The release declares each date exactly once, so a repeated row means the composer double-counted and every total is inflated.

rejection_cases.name: unanalysed dates are not in chronological order
rejection_cases.why: The page lists them as the release has them; a reversed list reads as a different history of refusals.

rejection_cases.name: an unanalysed date appears twice
rejection_cases.why: The release declares each date once; a repeat means the composer read a date twice.

rejection_cases.name: a date is both a run and unanalysed
rejection_cases.why: classify_date gives each date one alert_state. A date on both lists would show alerts and a refusal for the same day.

rejection_cases.name: the reasons of an unanalysed date are not in canonical order
rejection_cases.why: Shape-valid and semantically the same, but the index is reproducible byte for byte, so two composers that order differently disagree.

run_cases.name: empty run reports zeros and the pcount floor
run_cases.why: A date with no alerts is a valid observation of absence (GREEN_RELEASE_CONTRACT_V1 alert_state 'zero_alerts'), never to be collapsed into no-data. pcount_max must still be 1 or the UI slider range collapses.

run_cases.name: the three persistence tiers partition the features
run_cases.why: Boundaries at exactly CANDIDATE_MIN_SIGHTINGS and CONFIRMED_MIN_SIGHTINGS, plus one either side of each. An off-by-one in either comparison moves a feature between tiers.

run_cases.name: a missing streak counts as one sighting, not as a crash
run_cases.why: The producer writes null for a track it has not counted yet, and int(None) raises. 'Not counted' means seen once, which is what a first observation is.

run_cases.name: strong membership needs all three conjuncts
run_cases.why: One feature satisfies everything; the other three each fail exactly one conjunct. Dropping any conjunct from the policy makes one of them strong and this case fails.

run_cases.name: the natural-fraction threshold is inclusive at the boundary
run_cases.why: STRONG_MIN_NATURAL_FRACTION is a floor, not a strict bound. The value is rounded to three decimals first, so 0.4999 is below and 0.5 is in.

run_cases.name: the pre-2A.6 natural-fraction field is read as a fallback
run_cases.why: Tracked alert files span two annotation schemas. Reading only lc_natural_frac_10m would silently empty the strong subset for every older date.

run_cases.name: an unlabelled feature is counted low, never high
run_cases.why: A label the policy does not name — including a missing one — must land in the conservative bin. Counting it as high would advertise confidence the detector never claimed.

run_cases.name: a non-areal geometry is not a counted alert
run_cases.why: count is not len(features). A Point carries no area, and counting it would break the tier partition the validator checks.

run_cases.name: MultiPolygon counts and a null area contributes nothing
run_cases.why: The backend writes MultiPolygon for split clearings. A null area_ha must add 0.0 rather than raise, because the feature still exists and still belongs to a tier. This case also pins a cross-language trap: 7.25 rounds to 7.2 under Python's round() and to 7.3 under JavaScript's toFixed(1). The expected value is the Python one, because that is what the site has published since the first run and moving it would restate history.

run_cases.name: area is rounded once, to one decimal
run_cases.why: Three areas that only sum to a stable value if the rounding happens after the summation. Rounding each feature first drifts from the total the page adds up.
